prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Consult neurosurgery early for consideration of intraventricular antibiotic administration and external ventricular drain.
Consult ENT for cochlear-implant assessment as a potential portal of entry.

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with ventriculitis

differential.key_features: Lymphocyte-predominant CSF, normal-to-mildly elevated glucose, lower protein, lower CRP/procalcitonin — clinically distinguished by less toxic appearance
Temporal lobe MRI changes, seizures or focal deficits, lymphocytic CSF; HSV PCR required to exclude
Subacute onset, lymphocytic CSF, basilar enhancement, very low glucose — different tempo and pattern from this case
Typically in severely immunocompromised host; cryptococcal antigen and India ink exclude
Sudden thunderclap headache, xanthochromic CSF, hemorrhage on CT — none of these features present

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.

Ependymal enhancement, intraventricular debris, and restricted diffusion in the ventricular system indicate ventriculitis, which prolongs treatment and may require intraventricular antibiotic delivery.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

Culture positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae at 18 hours (penicillin MIC 0.06 ug/mL susceptible; ceftriaxone MIC <0.5 ug/mL susceptible). Latex agglutination positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae antigen. ME PCR panel positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae; all other targets not detected. CSF lactate markedly elevated at 11.2 mmol/L. Pattern of neutrophilic pleocytosis with markedly elevated protein and very low glucose is consistent with bacterial infection

metadata.clinical_notes: Straightforward case of pneumococcal meningitis in a patient with cochlear implant (known risk factor). Classic presentation with all cardinal features present. Complicated by septic shock, DIC, SIADH, and sensorineural hearing loss.
key_teaching_points: Cochlear implants confer increased risk of pneumococcal meningitis
Do not delay antibiotics for any reason in suspected bacterial meningitis
Adjunctive dexamethasone is most beneficial in pneumococcal meningitis
Hearing loss screening is mandatory in meningitis survivors

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ramirez is a 38-year-old right-handed Hispanic male who presents to the emergency department via ambulance after his wife called 911 when she found him confused and febrile at home. According to his wife, the patient was in his usual state of health until approximately 18 hours ago when he began complaining of a progressively worsening headache that he described as the worst of his life, initially starting at the back of his head and then becoming diffuse. He took ibuprofen 400 mg twice without relief. By yesterday evening he developed chills and his wife measured a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius at home. He vomited three times overnight and complained that the bedroom lights were too bright, pulling a pillow over his face. His wife noted that around 4 AM, approximately 10 hours before presentation, he began having difficulty following conversation, giving nonsensical answers to simple questions, and appeared to not know where he was. She attempted to give him more ibuprofen and water but he was unable to keep anything down. He had a recent upper respiratory tract infection approximately one week ago with nasal congestion and purulent rhinorrhea, for which he did not seek medical attention. He has a history of a right cochlear implant. His wife also reports that she noticed a rash of small reddish-purple spots on his chest and legs that developed overnight. He has not had any seizures, and there is no history of recent travel, tick exposure, or contact with anyone known to have meningitis. He received the pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13) at the time of cochlear implant placement 4 years ago but has not received a booster or PPSV23.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked neck stiffness with resistance to passive flexion. Positive Kernig sign bilaterally — resistance and pain with passive knee extension when hip is flexed to 90 degrees. Positive Brudzinski sign — involuntary hip and knee flexion with passive neck flexion. Petechial rash noted on trunk and proximal lower extremities. No tongue bite marks. No evidence of trauma.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to perform finger-to-nose or heel-to-shin testing reliably due to altered mental status and poor cooperation.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Pupils equal at 3 mm, sluggishly reactive to light bilaterally. Visual fields unable to assess reliably. Fundoscopic exam reveals bilateral papilledema with blurred disc margins. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements grossly conjugate, no obvious gaze deviation. CN V: Withdraws to light touch bilaterally. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest, grimaces symmetrically to noxious stimulation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact on left to voice; cochlear implant on right. CN IX/X: Gag reflex present bilaterally. CN XI: Not reliably assessed. CN XII: Tongue midline when protruded on command.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed; patient unable to stand due to altered consciousness and severe headache.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Somnolent, arousable to voice but drifts back to sleep. Glasgow Coma Scale 12 (E3 V4 M5). Oriented to person only; unable to state location or date. Speech is slow and dysarthric. Unable to sustain attention for serial sevens. Follows simple one-step commands intermittently. Unable to assess recall reliably due to altered sensorium.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone mildly increased in all four extremities. Moves all extremities spontaneously and to command, though slowly. Strength approximately 4/5 throughout upper and lower extremities bilaterally, limited by poor cooperation. No clear focal weakness. No pronator drift assessable given mental status.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, triceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 3+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Bilateral plantar responses are extensor (upgoing Babinski signs).
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to painful stimuli symmetrically in all four extremities. Light touch grossly intact bilaterally. Detailed sensory examination deferred due to altered mental status.
